idiom_name: prototype-dispatched `clone()` method (`Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(this))` + field copy); `structuredClone` for data graphs
implementation_notes: Dynamic dispatch is the language default, so the classic structure collapses into one method: subclasses override `clone()`, and a base implementation can give a shallow, prototype-preserving copy in a single expression - `Object.assign(Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(this)), this)`. What genuinely replaces the pattern is `structuredClone()` (deep, cycle-safe, built into runtimes since 2022) for plain data: it removes the need for clone methods entirely, but it cannot stand in for the pattern for class instances because the structured clone algorithm does not walk the prototype chain, so the result is a plain object with methods and `instanceof` gone. Use `clone()` methods for anything carrying behaviour or private fields; use `structuredClone`/spread for data.
pitfalls: `structuredClone(x)` throws `DataCloneError` for functions, DOM nodes, WeakMap/WeakSet and symbols, silently drops symbol-keyed properties and accessor descriptors, and does not walk the prototype chain: class instances come back as plain objects - use it for data, never as the class-copy mechanism.

Spread (`{...instance}`) and `Object.assign` copy own enumerable properties into a plain object: the prototype (and with it all methods) is lost for class instances, and private `#fields` are invisible to both spread and structuredClone, so the clone body must live inside the class.
The shallow clone above still shares nested mutable state (arrays, Maps, nested objects) with the original - deep copies need per-class recursion or a documented copy-on-write convention.
